macro: The newsletter is a thematic strategy piece on the AI sector rather than a broad daily market wrap. No specific index moves or overnight action are discussed. The focus is on structural capital market dynamics affecting AI spending.
rates_fed: No direct commentary on rates, Fed policy, yields, or the dollar is included in this edition.
market_outlook: Adam's view is cautious-to-bearish on the broader AI sector in the near term. The key catalyst to watch is the ability of Anthropic and OpenAI to access equity and debt markets on terms that bulls expect — if those IPO timelines or valuations disappoint, the ripple effects across AI spending and valuations could be significant.
bull_case: The largest players — including Meta and Musk's SpaceX — are aggressively expanding compute capacity, positioning to crowd out weaker vendors and capture share during the current turbulence. Underlying demand for AI remains structurally strong, and bulls argue the funding stress is temporary given that demand. A stabilization in equity and debt issuance markets could quickly restore the capital pool needed to sustain growth trajectories.
bear_case: AI capex is dramatically outpacing operating cash flow, making the sector dangerously dependent on external funding from equity and debt investors — and those markets are now less accommodating. A deteriorating issuance landscape will inevitably shrink aggregate spending across the ecosystem. Critically, much of the demand powering top-line AI metrics is itself funded by loss-making companies, creating a circular vulnerability. If Anthropic and OpenAI cannot come public on anticipated terms, it creates a double negative: less compute spending and a lower valuation benchmark for the entire sector.

company_items.summary: Anthropic is described as one of the two 'suns around which the whole AI world rotates.' If Anthropic cannot IPO on the timing and valuations anticipated by bulls, there will be negative fallout for the entire sector — less capital available for compute spending and a lower benchmark for AI valuations broadly.

OpenAI is the other central pillar of the AI ecosystem. Its ability to access public markets on favorable terms is critical; failure to do so would reduce compute spending and reprice sector valuations downward. A large portion of token consumption is driven by loss-making companies funded in part through OpenAI's ecosystem.

Meta tweaked up its 2026 capex budget and hinted at another large number in 2027, signaling aggressive investment to capitalize on weaker competitors being squeezed out. This positions Meta as one of the few players with balance sheet strength to crowd out underfunded AI vendors.

Elon Musk discussed bringing over 10 gigawatts of compute online next year for SpaceX, representing a massive acceleration of AI infrastructure build-out. SpaceX is using the current funding turmoil to press its advantage against weaker players, though the capital intensity of this strategy carries its own risk.

sectors: AI and technology infrastructure are under structural pressure as the capital markets funding the sector become less accommodating. The core problem is that capex dramatically outpaces operating cash flow, making the entire AI build-out dependent on continued investor largess. Compute capacity is technically fungible but repurposing it away from anchor customers like Anthropic and OpenAI would be a slow and painful process. The biggest, best-capitalized players are likely to consolidate share while smaller or loss-making vendors face existential funding risk.
tts_summary: Here is the key read for today — and this one is a thematic, big-picture piece on artificial intelligence that every trader with exposure to the sector needs to hear. The core argument is this: the fundamental problem weighing on AI right now is not demand — it is funding. Artificial intelligence is one of the most capital-intensive industries ever created, and capital expenditure across the sector is dramatically outpacing operating cash flow. That means the entire build-out is dependent on equity and debt investors continuing to write large checks — and those markets are now becoming significantly less accommodating. As the issuance landscape deteriorates, aggregate spending across the ecosystem will shrink. The pool of capital willing to underwrite everything is smaller than it was, and that matters enormously. Now, the largest players are responding by pressing harder — Meta raised its 2026 capex budget and is signaling another huge number in 2027. Musk is talking about bringing more than ten gigawatts of compute online next year for SpaceX. The strategy is straightforward: use their balance sheet strength to crowd out weaker, underfunded vendors. But here is the part that should concern bulls most. A significant chunk of the demand powering all those impressive top-line AI metrics — user growth, annualized recurring revenue, backlog — is itself coming from loss-making companies that are funded by the same capital markets now pulling back. That is a circular vulnerability, and it is not a small one. The two companies that matter most to this entire picture are Anthropic and OpenAI. These are the central pillars of the AI world. If either company cannot come public on the timing or valuations that bulls are counting on, the fallout is twofold: less money available to spend on compute infrastructure, and a lower valuation benchmark against which every other AI name gets repriced. Compute capacity is technically fungible — it can be repurposed — but that process is slow and painful, not a quick fix. The directional lean here is cautious to bearish on the broader AI sector near term. The bull case rests on funding stress being temporary and demand being strong enough to pull capital back in. The bear case is that the demand itself is partially a function of that funding — and if the funding dries up, the demand numbers will follow. Watch Anthropic and OpenAI market access closely. That is the signal.
